What clauses and Long Phrases as Subject
You shift emphasis from the beginning to another part of the sentence by using what , that and who phrases as subjects.

Usually, we focus on the person doing the action in this case.
Example: I think we should look at the sections of your resume next.

If we wish to place emphasis on another part of the sentence, we isolate that part and package up the rest of the information into a what-phrase (or sometimes a that clause.)
Example: What I think we should do next is look at the sections of your resume.

What or Who serves as a placeholder for the content of the noun phrase that has been moved to the end of the sentence. The effect is that more emphasis is placed on the initial content.
Example:
• What I don't understand is why you only have your contact information, your experience, and your hobbies.
This is how we form “What” clauses.

Resume Sections

Writing a resume can be a daunting experience, especially if you have never written one. There are certain rules that can be applied when it comes to organizing one. Not all resumes are the same, but here are some important sections that employers in a variety of industries will expect to see.

a. Header
Here you write your name in bold and in a font that is slightly larger than the rest of the resume.
Make sure you include your contact information (i.e. mailing address, phone number, and e-mail).

b. Objective Statement
Although this is optional, employers expect to see is a statement showing the direction you want to go. You can also include your work preferences.

c. Education
Here you add any information regarding your degree. Include where and when you graduated. You may include your GPA if it is strong.

d. Experience
Use either a chronological and combination formats. Make sure you add any relevant experience should be added. For example include jobs, internships, volunteer experiences and coursework.

e. References
Finally, make sure you include a reference section at the end of your resume. Simply indicate that your references are “available upon request”. Bear in mind that you should have at least three people who can serve as your references.

Adam: What's next?
Kristi: What I think we should do next is look at the sections of your resume. What I don't understand is why you only have your contact information, your experience, and your hobbies.
Adam: I thought this would suffice.
Kristi: Adam, what you want your resume to be is eye catching. There are certain sections that employers will expect to see.
Adam: Like what?
Kristi: I'd recommend adding a job objective statement.
Adam: Okay. What do I write about?

Kristi: What employers expect to see is a statement showing the direction you want to go. You can also include your work preferences.
Adam: Can I include skills I bring to the position? I could add some of those action verbs you mentioned.
Kristi: Absolutely. Another section you want to include is your education. In this section, you could add any information regarding your degree. Don't forget to include where and when you graduated.
Adam: Should I include my GPA?
Kristi: Only if it is an asset. If you feel your GPA isn't strong, make sure you put more of your non-academic experience with an emphasis on your strengths and skills.
Adam: Got it.
Kristi: I've also noticed you only listed your formal job experience.

Adam: I know. But those are the places where I gained all my prior experience.
Kristi: What about volunteer experience or unpaid experience? You could have them here as well.
Adam: I volunteered as a content editor for two university publications.
Kristi: Then, what I'd suggest is listing them here. Finally, make sure you include a reference section at the end of your resume.
Adam: Should I write their names and contact information as well?
Kristi: No, simply indicate that your references are “available upon request”. Bear in mind that you should have at least three people who can serve as your references.
Adam: Gotcha! Thanks, Kristi!
